QUESTION PRESENTED
Whether the Court should overrule Williams v.
Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970),  and hold that the Sixth
and Fourteenth Amendments  require the use of
12-person juries.

1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Utah Association of Counties is a statewide,
non-profit organization composed of the 29 counties of
Utah that aims to strengthen county government and
improve the well-being of Utah’s citizens.1
Amicus has a direct and substantial interest in
the question presented. Its members comprise
counties in one of the seven States that employ juries
of fewer than 12 in felony cases. For over half a
century, Utah has relied on this Court’s sound
decision in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970), to
organize its criminal justice system. Utah has built
courtrooms, jury boxes, and jury deliberation rooms to
accommodate juries of eight. Amicus’s member
counties have convicted thousands of murderers,
rapists, child abusers, and other violent criminals
with eight-member juries. Should the Court take the
extraordinary step of overruling Williams, those
counties would need to spend millions of dollars on
years of construction and  retrials, making difficult
decisions about which convicted criminals to allow to
plead out or let off scot-free. Those counties would also
have to persuade thousands of victims and witnesses
to once again relive the worst day of their lives.

1 Under Rule 37.6, no counsel for a party authored this brief in
whole or in part, and no person other than amicus curiae or its
counsel made a monetary contribution to its preparation or submission.

2
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Utah’s justice system is already strained. Just
last month, the presiding judge of Utah’s Third Judicial District —its most populous —alerted the bar to
“the unprecedented challenges that threaten to substantially alter local practice and delay justice.” Mow,
The State of the Third District, 39 Utah B.J. (Sep/Oct
2026) at 13, https://perma.cc/8DK9-KYSZ. The Third
District “is under extraordinary strain due to high
caseloads, a severe shortage of personnel and physical
space, new legislative mandates, and an imminent
surge in case filings from the closure of local justice
courts.” Id. Judge Mow report ed a 10% annual increase in jury trials, to 219; that “each judge, commissioner, and judicial assistant ” is working “114% of a
‘standard’ caseload”; that judges are working “nights
and weekends to keep up” but that it is “not sustainable”; and that the likely consequences will be “[s]cheduling many months in the future,” “[d]elays in … proposed judgments, orders, and oth er filings,” “fewer
hearings,” “time limits on civil and domestic hearings
and trials,” and “[s]tacking and bumping of civil and
domestic trials.” Id. at 13-14.
Overruling Williams would exacerbate th ose
challenges and inflict catastrophic damage on Utah’s
justice system. It could require overturning hundreds
of convictions currently on direct appeal ,
overwhelming State resources and endangering
public safety. As of October 2026, 251 criminal
appeals pending in Utah courts involved convictions
from juries of fewer than 12, including:

3
• 58 homicides averaging 5 days of trial
each, including 13 aggravated murders (25-
to-life or life without parole), 32 murders
(15-to-life), 4  attempted murders,
3 manslaughters, 1 negligent homicide ,
2 child abuse homicides, and 3 automobile
homicides;
• 43 sexual assaults  averaging 3.2 days of
trial each, including 19 rapes, 10 object
rapes, 6 forcible sex abuses, 4  aggravated
sexual assaults, and 4 forcible sodomies;
• 71 sexual assaults against children
averaging nearly 3 days of trial each,
including 14 child rapes, 41 aggravated
child sex abuses, 3 child sex abuses, 7  child
sodomies, 1 attempted child sodomy,
3 aggravated sex assaults of a child, and
2 sexual exploitations of a minor;
• 9 aggravated kidnappings , 1  aggravated human smuggling, and 2  unlawful detentions averaging nearly 3  days of
trial each;
• 1 child kidnapping and 2 instances of
child human trafficking  averaging
3.7 days of trial each; and
• 15 aggravated assaults averaging nearly
2 days of trial each.2
If these convictions are reversed because this
Court overrules Williams, the State must decide
which of these heinous crimes it can afford to retry—
and which it must allow to plead out or be dismissed

2 Utah Attorney General’s Office, Pending Appeals from Felony
Jury Trials, https://perma.cc/Q4ZD-VEE3.

4
entirely. Forty-seven of those convictions involved
offenses that occurred ten or more years ago; the
oldest is an aggravated child sex abuse case from
1991. For those cases where witnesses are still
available, victims and witnesses —including many
children—will suffer through months of pretrial
litigation before a second crucible of trial to reconvict
criminals already convicted by a unanimous jury of
their peers. Some dangerous criminals could be
released into the community pending retrial. The
following represents just a small sample of criminals
currently appealing their jury convictions:
• Jerrod Baum, who was found guilty of
kidnapping two teenagers, murdering them
with a knife in front of his girlfriend, and
dropping their bodies down an abandoned
mine shaft;
• Charles Tracy Camara, who was found
guilty of raping, sodomizing, and sexually
abusing a 13 -year-old girl he groomed
through an after-school soccer club;
• Fernando Flores, who was found guilty of
aggravated kidnapping, aggravated assault,
and domestic violence in the presence of a
child after holding  his girlfriend for three
days, smashing her face into a counter, and
burning her with boiling water while her
children were in the next room;
• Ross Wesley Lebaron, who was found guilty
of five counts of rape after he forced his
oldest daughter to marry him, rap ed her
almost weekly for twenty years, and caused
her to bear seven of his children; and

5
• Miguel Angel Leon Gomez, who was found
guilty of  raping and sodomizing his
coworker in a dairy farm shed on Halloween.
In short, reversing Williams would wreak untold
havoc on Utah’s already overburdened justice system.
And it would upend the lives of countless victims and
their families who believed they had finally received a
measure of justice and could move forward with their
lives.
No constitutional basis exists to upend Utah’s
criminal justice system  this way . Williams was
correctly decided . The Sixth Amendment expressly
guarantees just two jury features: that the jury will be
“impartial” and that the jurors will be drawn from “the
State and district wherein the crime shall have been
committed.” U.S. Const. amend. VI . Williams
surveyed th e “history and language of the
Constitution,” and “the reasoning of [the Court’s] past
decisions,” and concluded that not “every feature of
the jury as it existed at common law  … was
necessarily included in the Constitution wherever
that document referred to a ‘jury.’” 399 U.S. at 91, 103.
The Court then held that while the number of jurors
should be “large enough to promote group
deliberation, free from outside attempts at
intimidation, and to provide a fair possibility for
obtaining a representative cross -section of the
community,” a 12-person requirement was not
indispensable to “the essential feature of a jury .” Id.
at 100 . Americans receive their constitutional due
when six or more laymen “interpos[e] [themselves]
between the accused and … accuser” and provide “the
community participation and shared responsibility

6
that results from [their] determination of guilt or
innocence.” Id.
That analysis comports with the Court’s
originalist approach in interpreting other
constitutional provisions. Petitioner’s historical
evidence—much of it the same Williams found
lacking—does not undermine the Court’s conclusion
that the Constitution permits six-member juries.
Even if Williams were wrongly decided, the
Court should affirm it as a matter of stare decisis .
Williams is not “egregiously wrong.” Dobbs v. Jackson
Women’s Health Org. , 597 U.S. 215, 268 (2022).  The
“‘quality’ of [its] reasoning” is high. Trump v.
Slaughter, 146 S.Ct. 2283, 2302  (2026). It is
“‘consisten[t]” with the Court’s other cases. Id. Its rule
is “workab[le].” Id. And the reliance interests at stake
are enormous.  Finally, because the question
presented turns on a  historical query, “something
more than ‘ambiguous historical evidence’ is required
before [the Court] will ‘flatly overrule ’” this  “‘major
decision[].’” Gamble v. United States , 587 U.S. 678,
691 (2019) . A party seeking such a change bears a
“particular burden under stare decisis” to “settl[e] the
historical question with enough force.” See id. at 699-
700. Petitioner has not “come close” to meeting it. Id.

7
ARGUMENT
I. Williams was correctly decided.
A. Williams surveyed the historical record
to determine the Sixth Amendment’s
original public meaning.
The Sixth Amendment provides: “In all criminal
prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right to a
speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury of the
State and district wherein the crime shall have been
committed.” U.S. Const. amend. VI. Its plain text thus
guarantees just two jury features: that the jury will be
“impartial” and that jurors will be drawn from “the
State and district wherein the crime shall have been
committed.” Id. So when the Framers codified the jury
right, they omitted not only  the traditional vicinage
requirement but also —unlike many State
constitutions and statutes —other traditional
common-law jury characteristics such as number and
property requirements. See Resp.Br.15, 25-27.
Petitioner and several amici echo Justice
Harlan’s accusation that Williams “gave no weight to
the historical record.” See, e.g., Pet.Br.2. But that
reading of Williams is untenable. As several members
of the Court have already recognized, Williams
“engag[ed] in a detailed discussion of the original
meaning of the Sixth Amendment jury -trial right.”
Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 152 (2020) (Alito, J.,
dissenting).
Williams began by referencing the extensive
historical analysis the Court conducted just two years

8
earlier in Duncan v. Louisiana , 391 U.S. 145 (1968) ,
which incorporated the criminal jury right against the
States. 399 U.S. at 8 6-87. But c oncluding that that
history “afford[ed] little insight into the
considerations that gradually led the size of th[e] body
to be generally fixed at 12,”  Williams analyzed still
more sources. Id. at 87.
In doing so, it consulted Lord Coke, James
Thayer, and other scholars from the nineteenth and
twentieth centuries that discussed the ancient right.
After a  lengthy, careful analysis,  see id.  at 87 -90 &
nn.19-25, t he Court concluded there was no
satisfactory answer for where the number 12 had
come from, and that this “particular feature of the jury
system appears to have been a historical accident,
unrelated to the great purposes which gave rise to the
jury in the first place,” id. at 89-90.
Next, the Court reviewed its previous opinions,
which had “assumed” this historical accident had been
“immutably codified into our Constitution.” Id. at 90.
It found very little analysis in those opinions. Instead,
they largely quoted passages noting that “at common
law the jury did indeed consist of 12.” Id. at 91. Again,
the Court carefully consulted academic sources and
documented its conclusions in a series of lengthy
footnotes. See id. at 90-92 & nn.26-31.
The Court then sought to discern “‘the intent of
the Framers’” to determine whether “if a given feature
existed in a jury at common law in 1789, then it was
necessarily preserved in the Constitution.” Id. at 92.
The Court consulted the Constitution’s original jury
guarantee in Article III , the records of the

9
Constitutional Convention , Blackstone, James
Madison’s personal correspondence , and the Sixth
Amendment’s legislative history. Id. at 92-96 & nn.32-
41.
Only then did the Court observe “[t]hree
significant features” in “the background of the
Constitution’s jury trial provisions”: (1) “even though
the vicinage requirement was as much a feature of the
common-law jury as was the 12-man requirement, the
mere reference to ‘t rial by jury’ in Article III was not
interpreted to include that feature”; (2) “[p]rovisions
that would have explicitly tied the ‘jury’ concept to the
‘accustomed requisites’ of the time were eliminated”;
and (3)  “contemporary legislative and constitutional
provisions indicate that where Congress wanted to
leave no doubt that it was incorporating existing
common-law features of the jury system, it knew how
to use express language to that effect.” Id. at 96-97 &
nn.42-44. On the last point, the Court compared the
language of the Sixth Amendment to the language of
the Seventh Amendment , as well as that of the
Judiciary Act and other early legislation. Id.
After “examining that history,” the Court
concluded “the Sixth Amendment did not incorporate
every feature of the common -law right.” Ramos, 590
U.S. at 152 (Alito, J., dissenting).  Ramos did not
dispute this fundamental holding, id., and Williams
has been repeatedly reaffirmed since 1970, infra at 26.
B. Williams has withstood the test of time.
Petitioner asserts that the phrase trial by an
impartial jury  “‘unmistakabl[y]’” “referred to a 12 -

10
person jury at the time the Sixth Amendment was
enacted.” Pet.Br.18 -19. And one amicus claims
“historical materials unknown or unavailable to the
[Williams] Court” make it “plain” the Framers “used
a settled legal term that meant twelve.” Su.Br.2-3.
Those contentions are overstated. First,
substantial evidence —including evidence cited by
Petitioner—confirms that the Founders understood
jury to refer to panels of fewer than 12. Second,
Petitioner’s case law does not establish jury required
12. Third, evidence from the Carolinas does not
contradict Williams. And fourth, the fact that a 12 -
member body may have formed part of the usual jury
does not mean that the Framers constitutionalized
that number.
1. Jury did not invariably mean “12 men.”  Just
three years after Williams, the Court cited additional
scholarship to conclude that “[a]lthough Williams
proceeded on the premise that the common -law jury
was composed of 12 members, juries of less than 12
were common in this country throughout colonial
times.” Colgrove v. Battin , 413 U.S. 149, 158 n.12
(1973) (citing Fisher, The Seventh Amendment and the
Common Law: No Magic in Numbers , 56 F.R.D. 507,
529-32 (1973)). For example, between 1665 and 1699,
New York law provided that “No Jury shall exceed the
number of Seaven nor be under Six unless in Special
Causes upon Life and Death, The Justices shall thinke
fitt to Appoint twelve.” 1 Lyon, The Colonial Laws of
New York from the Year 1664 to the Revolution  6, 42
(1896). Pennsylvania was governed by  the same law
until 1682. See Fisher, supra, at 529. In 1769, citizens
of North Carolina petitioned, albeit unsuccessfully, for

11
juries of six. Id. at 530. And there are other examples.
Id. at 529-32; Resp.Br.13-15. Famously, the civil jury
right varied so much across the States that the
Framers initially opted not to guarantee the right at
all. See The Federalist No. 83 (Alexander Hamilton).
This diversity of practice explains why some of
Petitioner’s own sources  equivocate. See Pet.Br.8-9
(Samuel Spencer: “[C]ases which affect … lives and
property, are to be decided, in a great measure, by the
consent of twelve honest disinterested men”)
(emphasis added); id. at 10 (Justice Joseph Story:
“trial by jury is generally understood to mean … a trial
by a jury of twelve men”) (emphasis altered); id. (Joel
Tiffany: “a trial by jury is understood to mean —
generally—a trial by a jury of twelve men”) (emphasis
added). Indeed, Samuel Spencer was not arguing that
the Constitution preserved a 12-juror requirement but
describing how a country could avoid being
“enslaved.” 4 The Debates in the Several State
Conventions on the Adoption of the Federal
Constitution 154 (J. Elliot ed., 2d ed. 1836) (“Elliot’s”).
Far from acknowledging jury had a settled legal
meaning, Spencer argued it was “highly improper that
any clause which regards the security of the trial by
jury should be any way doubtful ,” and objected that
the Constitution  was not “sufficiently explicit” to
preserve vicinage. Id.
The Colonies’ vari ed practices also explain  why,
by Petitioner’s count , five States at ratification had
laws or constitutional provisions “expressly
referencing 12 -member juries.” Pet.Br.7. If jury had
been universally understood to mean a body of 12,
those States would not have needed to so clarify. But

12
because t he States had experimented with different
jury sizes, any State that prized the common number
had to expressly guarantee it. See also id. at 6
(“Twelve-member juries were fixtures in at least most
of the American colonies at the time of the founding.”)
(emphasis added).
2. Early case law likewise fails to establish that
impartial jury necessarily codified 12-member panels.
Petitioner and his amici place much stock in the 1780
New Jersey decision of Holmes v. Walton. See Pet.Br.7
n.2; Su.Br.19-20; ACLU.Br.10; USCCB.Br.16. But no
opinion accompanying the judgment in that case has
ever been found. Scott, Holmes vs. Walton: The New
Jersey Precedent , 4 Am. Hist. Rev. 456, 459 (1899) .
And while it seems clear the court held a jury of six
was not “constitutional,” State v. Parkhurst, 9 N.J.L.
427, 444 (1802), the basis for this holding is not clear
at all. One scholar, after canvassing counsel’s various
jury-related arguments, argued that “[t]he
assumption that the [1776 New Jersey Constitution’s]
phrase ‘trial by jury’ … meant exactly twelve jurors
must find its warrant farther back .” Scott, supra, at
457-59 (emphasis added) . See also id.  at 459
(identifying express 12 -man requirements in  other
fundamental-law documents like the West Jersey
Concessions and Agreements of 1676 and the East
Jersey Rights and Privileges of 1699 ). Because the
court’s rationale is unknown, the more important —
and only concrete—takeaway from this episode is that
the Founding Era New Jersey legislature repeatedly
passed laws permitting six -man juries : in February
1775, October 1778, and December 1779 . Id. at 456-
57, 461-62. The first allowed a party in an action
involving forty shillings to  six pounds to “demand a

13
Jury,” whereupon “six good and lawful Men of the
County, being Freeholders” should be sworn, hear the
evidence, and “be kept together in some convenient
private Place … till they all agree upon a Verdict.”
Acts of the General Assembly of the Province of New -
Jersey, from the Surrender of the Government to Queen
Anne, on the 17th Day of April, in the Year of our Lord
1702, to the 14th Day of January 1776  469-70
(S. Allinson ed. 1776). The last two were aimed at
preventing “illicit trade with the British ”—a crime
“tantamount to treason”—and yet the second “passed
both houses without a dissenting vote. ” Scott, supra,
at 461.
Nor is  Petitioner correct  that “[i]n the decades
after the Sixth Amendment was ratified, state courts
uniformly held that the term ‘trial by jury’ in their
own constitutions required 12 jurors .” Pet.Br.9; see
also id. at 19-21. To start, the defendant in Zylstra v.
Corporation of City of Charleston  received no jury at
all. 1 S.C.L. 382, 376 (Ct. Com. Pl. 1794). Same for the
defendant in Emerick v. Harris , 1 Binn. 416, 416 -17
(Pa. 1808). Regardless, neither court interpreted trial
by jury to require 12 jurors. In Zylstra, a single justice
opined that:
[W]hen the rights of the citizens are to be
determined on by 12 men …
indiscriminately drawn from every class of
their fellow citizens, there will be a better
chance generally, that the poor will receive
an equal measure of justice with the rich,
and that the decision of facts wil l be
according to the truth of them.

14
1 S.C.L. at 389 (op. of Waties, J.).
And in Emerick, one justice stated only that
William Penn’s charter of liberties (declaring in part
that “all trials shall be by twelve men”) was “the same,
in substance,” to jury provisions in the  longsuperseded 1776 Pennsylvania Constitution.  1 Binn.
at 426 (op. of Brackenridge, J.).  Far from finding the
1790 Pennsylvania Constitution imposed a  12-man
requirement, Justice Brackenridge joined the court in
upholding the constitutionality of a law that enlarged
the jurisdiction of jury-less justices of the peace. Id. at
428.
As for Whitehurst v. Davis, the court interpreted
a provision guaranteeing the “ancient mode of trial by
jury” to prohibit a verdict by 13 jurors. 3 N.C. 113, 113
(1800) (emphasis added). And unlike this Court’s
unchallenged determination that the Sixth
Amendment did not codify every aspect of the
common-law jury, the North Carolina court reached
its decision only by concluding that “any innovation
amounting in the least degree to a departure from the
ancient mode” was impermissible. Id. Notably, North
Carolina had statutes stipulating twelve. See, e.g.,
Acts of the North Carolina General Assembly, 1779 ,
24 Colonial & St. Recs. N.C. 269  (“a jury of twelve
freeholders”).
Petitioner’s 1848 cases are similarly unavailing.
Pet.Br.9. Larillian v. Lane & Co. discussed the
“constitution of the country,” found it permitted no
deviation from the common-law jury, and determined
it was precisely the text’s silence that mandated a
specific number of jurors . 8 Ark. 372, 374 -75 (1848).

15
And Larillian did not hold that a verdict of eleven was
no verdict at all: “ If the jury really did not consist of
twelve men, and the defendant … did not intend to
waive his constitutional rights, he should have
reserved the point …, and then it would have been
entitled to … consideration.” Id. at 375. Rouse v. State
interpreted not impartial jury , but a provision
guaranteeing that “trial by jury, as heretofore used in
this State, shall remain inviolate.” 4 Ga. 136, 145
(1848) (cleaned up).  Georgia’s first constitution had
stipulated “the first twelve” names “drawn out” “shall
be the special jury to try the cause.” Ga. Const.  of
1777, art. 40. And any comment on twelve jurors was
dicta: the question presented was whether a grand
juror—allegedly not a “peer” of the accused —could
serve as a petit juror in a criminal trial. Rouse, 4 Ga.
at 137, 147-48.
The cases Petitioner cites  to show  state courts
continued to affirm “the need for 12 ” throughout the
nineteenth century, Pet.Br.9, likewise shed little light
on the Sixth Amendment’s original public meaning.
An “equally divided” Alabama court opined, without
referring to any constitutional or statutory provision,
that “[t]he term jury is well understood to be twelve
men” and acknowledged parties could consent to less.
Foote v. Lawrence, 1 Stew. 483, 483-84 (Ala. 1828). An
Ohio court interpreted two jury provisions of the 1851
state constitution to invalidate a six -man criminal
jury, over a dissent and despite a separate
constitutional provision expressly requiring “a jury of
twelve men” in eminent domain cases . Work v. State,
2 Ohio St. 296, 30 1-02, 307 -08 (1853). It assumed
incorrectly that the language of the jury trial right
had “ages of uninterrupted use”  and that “[u]ntil

16
passage of th[e] law, no person had ever been
convicted of crime by less … and no law ha[d] ever
attempted to authorize it .” Id. at 30 2, 305 . It also
declined to extend th at holding to civil cases . Id. at
307. In a capital case, a New York court held that the
defendant could not consent to a jury of eleven, in light
of the common law ; a constitutional provision
declaring that “ ‘trial by jury, in all cases in which it
has heretofore been used, shall remain inviolate
forever’”; and a specific statutory provision providing
“that the twelve first jurors who shall appear on being
called, and be approved as indifferent, shall constitute
the jury .” Cancemi v. People , 18 N.Y. 128, 135, 138
(1858). A Missouri court invalidated a six -man jury
verdict while acknowledging a party might not always
“afterwards avail himself of [such] error” and could
always consent to six jurors. Vaughn v. Scade, 30 Mo.
600, 603 -04 (1860).  That court also held, without
explanation, that “[o]f course the non -essentials of
th[e] institution, such as concern the qualification of
jurors, the mode of summoning them, and many other
such matters, were left to the regulation of law.” Id. at
604. And it clarified that a “jury in a justice’s court”
could use “any number of men that is deemed
expedient.” Id. at 604 -05. Finally, in an advisory
opinion “regret[fully]” given without “the usual aid
from the investigations of interested parties and their
learned counsel,” a New Hampshire court erroneously
assumed that “ ‘jury’” and “ ‘trial by jury ’” were
“always” used “in a single sense” before the adoption
of the constitution, and that “[a]t that date, … no such
thing as a jury of less than twelve men … had ever
been known, or ever been the subject of discussion in

17
any country of the common law .” Opinion of Justices,
41 N.H. 550, 550-52 (1860).
3. Professor Su’s Carolina  evidence fares no
better. She asserts that “[t]he Carolinas’ constitutions
presupposed that a jury had twelve.” Su.Br.7. But as
she immediately  points out, the 1669 Fundamental
Constitutions of Carolina “expressly codified the right
to a jury of twelve.” Id. And still,  Zylstra did not
interpret South Carolina’s later constitution to
require 12 jurors. Supra, at 13.
Professor Su also claims an 1844  decision
“unequivocal[ly]” held that “[t]he words ‘trial by jury’
in the South Carolina Constitution” meant twelve
jurors. Su.Br.8-10. But this decision came more than
50 years after the ratification of the Sixth
Amendment. More to the point,  that was not the
court’s holding:
It is next necessary to test … what is meant
“by the judgment of his peers” and “the trial
by jury, as heretofore used in this State,
shall be forever inviolably preserved.”  The
“judgment of his peers” means in general the
great unalienable common law mode of trial
by twelve good and lawful men  of the
vicinage, in the presence of the accused, and
by the oath of a witness. And the words “the
trial by jury, as heretofore used in this State,
shall be forever inviolably preserved,”  mean
that in all cases where it had not been
previously abandoned, it should be
continued to every freeman, and of course to
every woman and child….

18
State v. Simons , 29 S.C.L.  761, 768 (Ct. Err. 1844 )
(emphasis added).
In sum, a state court (1) found 12 jurors were “in
general” required  by the phrase “judgment of his
peers,” (2) by a  state constitution that specifically
“inviolably preserved” a jury right “as heretofore used
in th [e] State,” (3) where a previous founding
document expressly guaranteed 12.  None of that
reveals anything about the original public meaning of
impartial jury in the Sixth Amendment. Even the
pronouncement that the slave panel was “not a trial
by jury, in any sense in which the words have ever
been legally used,” fails to confirm the court’s decision
turned on number , as the challenged “forum” also
included two magistrates.  Id. And the “essential
feature of a jury obviously lies in the interposition
between the accused and his accuser of the
commonsense judgment of a group of laymen.”
Williams, 399 U.S. at 100.  See also  1 Elliot’s 504
(Richard Henry Lee quoting Blackstone’s warning
that “[i]f t[he administration of justice] be entirely
intrusted to the magistracy … these decisions … will
have frequently an involuntary bias towards those of
their own rank and dignity”).  All this confirms only
that “when it comes to interpreting the Constitution,
not all history is created equal. ” NYSRPA v. Bruen ,
597 U.S. 1, 34 (2022).
4. To be sure, the usual meaning of jury at the
time of the Founding may have contemplated twelve
jurors. Or more accurately—twelve white, male,
property-owning neighbors. See Resp.Br.25-27. But
the fact that  some in the Founding generation may
have had a particular iteration of a jury in mind does

19
not prove that the Sixth Amendment’s text
constitutionalized that top-of-mind sense.
For example, it would have been “‘unthinkable,’”
Khorrami v. Arizona, 143 S.Ct. 22, 25 (2022) (Gorsuch,
J., dissenting from denial of certiorari), at the time of
the Founding to have a pauper sit on a jury. See
Resp.Br.25-27. It may have been just as unthinkable
to have a jury composed entirely of individuals who
knew nothing  of the accused or the offense.  In the
Virginia Ratifying Convention, Patrick Henry argued
that by “ancient common law, the trial of all facts is
decided by a jury of impartial men from the immediate
vicinage” and that allowing jurors to be pulled from
the state at large was “extremely dangerous to liberty”
because “a person accused may be carried from o ne
extremity of the state to another, and be tried, not by
an impartial jury of the vicinage, acquainted with his
character and the circumstances of the fact , but by a
jury unacquainted with both, and who may be biased
against him.” 3 Elliot’s 446-47 (emphasis added) .
Blackstone’s oft -quoted line similarly contemplated
more than unanimity from a random group of twelve:
“[T]he truth of every accusation … should … be
confirmed by the unanimous suffrage of twelve of his
equals and neighbo urs.” 4 W. Blackstone,
Commentaries on the Laws of England  343 (1769)
(emphasis added).
The Founding generation valued certain jury
features—such as vicinage—at least as much as it
valued a certain number of jurors. See Williams, 399
U.S. at 96.  Indeed, the lack of specificity regarding
this timeless common-law jury feature, not a specific
number of jurors, caused Patrick Henry to exclaim:

20
Is not this sufficient to alarm men? How
different is this from the immemorial
practice of your British ancestors, and your
own! I need not tell you that, by the common
law, a number of hundredors were required
on a jury, and that afterwards it was
sufficient if the j urors came from the same
county. With less than this the people of
England have never been satisfied.
3 Elliot’s 447. “That paper,” Henry concluded
derisively, “ought to have declared the common law in
force.” Id. For his part, Richard Henry Lee viewed the
loss of the vicinage requirement and the possibility of
being tried in a “distant court”—not the possibility of
fewer jurors —as the “weaken[ing]” of the “great
security of human rights,” “the trial by jury.” 1 Elliot’s
504.
And yet no one contends that requirements such
as vicinage and freeholding were constitutionalized in
the simple phrase (notably stripped down by the
Senate) of “an impartial jury of the State and district
wherein the crime shall have been committed.” U.S.
Const. amend. VI. In short, nothing since Williams—
including Ramos—has even hinted that the Court was
wrong when it concluded “the Sixth Amendment did
not incorporate every feature of the common -law
right.” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 152 (Alito, J., dissenting).

21
C. Williams followed the same principled
approach as this Court’s decisions
interpreting other constitutional
provisions.
The Court has repeatedly declined to define the
scope of constitutional rights at the bounds of how the
Founders might have originally expected them to
apply. See, e.g., Chatrie v. United States , 146 S.Ct.
2193, 2222  (2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring  in the
judgment) (“As with other laws, the terms found in the
Fourth Amendment carry their original public
meaning and can bear more applications than its
drafters might have expected or intended.”). That’s
why “the First Amendment protects speech over the
internet today no less than it did speech delivered in
the town square in 1791,” id., and why “the Second
Amendment is not limited only to those arms that
were in existence at the founding,” United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 691 (2024).
Just as the Court has recognized that the
Constitution protects activities and technologies that
did not exist at the time of the Founding, it has
recognized that the Constitution does not trap all
features of eighteenth -century law “in amber.” Id. at
691. The Second Amendment, for example, “permits
more than just those regulations identical to ones that
could be found in 1791.” Id.; see also id . (“Holding
otherwise would be as mistaken as applying the
protections of the right only to muskets and sabers.”).
The Court has gone so far as to recognize that “the
regulatory challenges posed by firearms today are not
always the same as those earlier generations faced,”
and held that the Government need not point to a

22
“historical twin” or “precise historical precursor” to
justify a firearm regulation. United States v. Hemani,
608 U.S. 772, 780 (2026) (cleaned up).  Instead, “‘the
appropriate analysis involves considering whether the
challenged regulation is consistent with the principles
that underpin our regulatory tradition.’” Id. In other
words, even if a criminal procedure practice “is of
recent origin , this fact  hardly renders it
unconstitutional.” Payne v. Tennessee , 501 U.S. 808,
821 (1991).
After surveying the history, Williams asked
whether Florida’s six-member jury  violated “the
essential feature of a jury” —“the interposition
between the accused and his accuser of the
commonsense judgment of a group of laymen” of a
large enough number “to promote group deliberation,
free from outside attempts at intimidation, and to
provide a fair possibility for obtaining a
representative cross -section of the community.” 399
U.S. at 100.  That’s consistent with this Court’s
originalist text-and-history approach in other areas of
the law.
It bears repeating that the  Sixth Amendment
says nothing about a requisite number of jurors. It
guarantees “an impartial jury.” U.S. Const. amend.
VI. And again , other requirements such as vicinage
were “as much a feature of the common-law jury as …
the 12 -man requirement” but not considered to be
captured by “trial by jury.” Williams, 399 U.S. at 96.
So—then as now —concluding that something was a
“common-law characteristi[c] of [a] jury ,” id. at 99,
doesn’t suffice to answer the question presented.

23
Despite Petitioner’s best efforts to make it appear
otherwise, Pet.Br.2 5-27, Williams is not the Sixth
Amendment equivalent of Trop v. Dulles, which held
the Eighth Amendment “draw[s] its meaning from the
evolving standards of decency that mark the progress
of a maturing society” and spawned a jurisprudence of
fifty-state surveys. 356 U.S. 86, 101 (1958)  (op. of
Warren, C.J.) . Williams took it as a given that the
Sixth Amendment codified and preserved a defined
right. Williams just recognized, after a careful and
thorough historical survey, that the Sixth
Amendment did not codify every aspect of the
common-law jury. No one disputes t hat point. And
nothing since Williams has shown that the Sixth
Amendment incorporated a specific number of jurors,
any more than it incorporated vicinage or property
requirements.
II. The Court should affirm Williams as a
matter of stare decisis.
As a longstanding precedent, Williams is entitled
to stare decisis respect and should be affirmed on that
basis alone. “Stare decisis ‘promotes the evenhanded,
predictable, and consistent development of legal
principles, fosters reliance on judicial decisions, and
contributes to the actual and perceived integrity of the
judicial process.’” Gamble, 587 U.S. at 691.
“Accordingly, an argument that [the Court] got
something wrong —even a good argument to that
effect—cannot by itself justify scrapping settled
precedent.” Kimble v. Marvel Ent., LLC, 576 U.S. 446,
455 (2015). “[I]t is not alone sufficient that [the Court]
would decide a case differently now than [it] did then.”
Id. “[E]ven in constitutional cases, a departure from

24
precedent ‘demands special justification.’” Gamble,
587 U.S. at 691.  Accord Ramos , 590 U.S. at 120
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring  in part ). That’s because
“to ‘overrule an important precedent is serious
business.’” Id.; see also  Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 266-67;
Kimble, 576 U.S. at 455.
When deciding whether to overrule a precedent ,
this Court first considers whether the precedent is not
just wrong, but “‘egregiously wrong.’” Dobbs, 597 U.S.
at 268 (quoting Ramos, 590 U.S. at 121 (Kavanaugh,
J., concurring in part)). See also Ramos, 590 U.S. at
135 (Thomas, J., concurring  in the judgment )
(challenged precedent must be “demonstrably
erroneous”). If the question presented turns on a
historical question, “something more than ‘ambiguous
historical evidence’ is required before [the Court] will
‘flatly overrule a number of major decisions.’” Gamble,
587 U.S. at 691.  A petitioner seeking such a change
bears a “particular burden under stare decisis ” to
“settl[e] the historical question with enough force.” Id.
at 700.
Even if the Court is satisfied that a past
precedent is egregiously wrong, the Court considers a
number of other factors , including the “quality of the
decision’s reasoning, its consistency with [the Court’s]
other cases, the workability of its rule, and the
interests of those who have relied on it.” Slaughter,
146 S.Ct. at 2302  (cleaned up).  Here, every factor
favors preserving Williams.

25
A. Williams is entitled to respect as a
matter of stare decisis.
By any measure, the Court should conduct a stare
decisis analysis before  overruling a 56-year-old
precedent. But P etitioner highlights just how
decisively that analysis cuts against him by urging the
Court to  “not engage in the traditional stare decisis
inquiry at all” because Ramos “effectively overruled
Williams.” Pet.Br.15.
That argument lacks merit. The Ramos majority
cited Williams exactly once—in a footnote—to note a
quotation from Apodaca v. Oregon , 406 U.S. 404
(1972), itself quoted Williams. See Ramos, 590 U.S. at
99 n.41. An opinion that so assiduously avoid ed discussing Williams cannot have overruled it. To be sure,
three Justices in Ramos embraced an argument similar to  Petitioner’s: that Apodaca did not “suppl[y] a
governing precedent.” Id. at 101 (op. of Gorsuch, J .).
But six other Justices rejected that position. Id. at 125
n.6 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring  in part ) (“ [S]ix Justices treat the result in Apodaca as precedent for purposes of stare decisis analysis.”).
Regardless, Williams shares none of Apodaca’s
unique infirmities . Williams has never been an
unknowable constitutional outlier. See Ramos , 590
U.S. at 93 (majority op.)  (“Ultimately, the [ Apodaca]
Court could do no more than issue a badly fractured
set of opinions.”); id. at 95-96 & n.36 (plurality op.)
(Court had  been “studiously ambiguous, even
inconsistent, about what Apodaca might mean”  and
issued “‘reiterations’” “suggest[ing] different things at
different times”).

26
Instead, Williams issued a clear holding in an
opinion endorsed by a five-Justice majority of the
Court. Just one Justice believed the Constitution
requires the States to provide 12 -member juries. See
399 U.S. at 116-17 (Marshall, J., dissenting in part).
And the Court has repeatedly applied,
reaffirmed, and reasoned from Williams. See, e.g.,
United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506, 510 n.2 (1995);
Collins v. Youngblood , 497 U.S. 37, 53 n.4 (1990) ;
Holland v. Illinois, 493 U.S. 474, 478 (1990); Batson v.
Kentucky, 476 U.S. 79, 8 5 n.6 (1986); Crist v. Bretz ,
437 U.S. 28, 37 (1978); Ludwig v. Massachusetts, 427
U.S. 618, 625 (1976) ; Taylor v. Louisiana , 419 U.S.
522, 526-28 (1975); Colgrove, 413 U.S. at 151 -52.
Colgrove even extended Williams to hold that the
Seventh Amendment likewise does not require twelve
jurors. 413 U.S. at 151-60.
B. Williams is not egregiously wrong or
demonstrably erroneous.
Williams was correctly decided. No one today
believes the Sixth Amendment codified every feature
of the common -law jury , and the Court correctly
concluded that it did not codify a specific number of
jurors.
But even if Williams ultimately reached the
wrong conclusion with respect to jury size, nothing in
the historical record suggests its decision was
“‘egregiously wrong .’” Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 268.  That
may be why only one Justice believed Williams was
wrongly decided at the time, and why only one other
Justice has expressly called for it to be reconsidered

27
since. Even now, 56 years later, Petitioner relies
largely on the same historical evidence that Williams
found lacking. And none of it “come[s] close to settling
the historical question with enough force to meet
[Petitioner’s] particular burden under stare decisis .”
Gamble, 587 U.S. at 699-700.
Overruling Williams simply because the Court
now has a slightly different view of the Constitutional
Convention, or the Senate’s deletion of specific
protections from James Madison’s original bill, would
break significant new ground. See Kimble, 576 U.S. at
455 (“Respecting stare decisis means sticking to some
wrong decisions .… Indeed, stare decisis has
consequence only to the extent it sustains incorrect
decisions.”). Williams explicitly acknowledged
contrary view s on the history and admitted that it
“d[id] not pretend to be able to divine precisely what
the word ‘jury’ imported to the Framers, the First
Congress, or the States in 1789.”  399 U.S. at 96 -98.
That same humility warrants adhering to the Court’s
rule here that “‘ambiguous historical evidence’” is not
enough to overturn a “‘major decision[] of this Court.’”
Gamble, 587 U.S. at 691.
C. The quality of Williams’s reasoning is
high.
Far from giving “short shrift to original meaning
and precedent,” Khorrami, 143 S.Ct. at 26 (Gorsuch,
J., dissenting from denial of certiorari) , Williams extensively surveyed the historical record o n the jury
guarantee. Supra, at 7-9. It also accurately described
earlier decisions as “assum[ing] an affirmative answer” to the Sixth Amendment question  and

28
“reaffirm[ing]” those pronouncements “often in dictum
and usually by relying—where there was any discussion of the issue at all—solely on the fact that the common-law jury consisted of 12.” 399 U.S. at 90 -92
(cleaned up).  That’s why Justice Harlan largely resorted to accusing the majority of “cavalier disregard”
for “pronouncements … that reflect[ed] [an] understanding,” defending the “significance” of just one
such “pronouncement” in a footnote. Baldwin v. New
York, 399 U.S. 117, 126 -27 & n.12 (1970) (Harlan, J.,
concurring in the result in Williams).
Petitioner accuses Williams of engaging in an
“incomplete functionalist analysis.” Pet.Br. 29
(cleaned up). But at no point di d Williams engage in
some “judge-empowering interest-balancing inquiry,”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 22  (cleaned up), or hold that the
needs of contemporary society could outweigh
constitutional guarantees. Instead, it reviewed the
history and concluded “there is absolutely no
indication in ‘the intent of the Framers’ of an explicit
decision to equate the constitutional and common-law
characteristics of the jury.” Williams, 399 U.S. at 99.
Then, rather than hold that the States could do
whatever they wanted with respect to the number of
jurors, the Court “turn[ed] to other than purely
historical considerations to determine which features
of the jury system, as it existed in common law, were
preserved in the Constitution.” Id. (emphasis added).
The Court ultimately determined that any jury must
“interpos[e] between the accused and his accuser …
the commonsense judgment of a group of laymen” and
preserve “the community participation and shared
responsibility that results from that group’s
determination of guilt or innocence.” Id. at 100. The

29
Court then intimated that the Constitution limited
how much a State could shrink a jury. See id.
Nor does Ramos’s basis for overruling Apodaca
apply to Williams. Ramos found Apodaca’s reasoning
was poor in part because it failed to “grappl[e] with …
the racist origins of Louisiana’s and Oregon’s laws.”
590 U.S. at 106.  But elsewhere the Court suggested
the laws’ allegedly racist histor ies were irrelevant to
the analysis. See id. at 99 n.44 (stating the Court was
merely “acknowledging the racist history of [the]
laws” and that “adopting a nonunanimous jury rule
even for benign reasons would still violate the Sixth
Amendment”). And three Justices denied such
allegedly racist history could factor into the stare
decisis analysis. Id. at 14 1-42, 153  (Alito, J.,
dissenting).
At any rate, in Ramos, the only States still
accepting nonunanimous jury verdicts were two that
had allegedly originated the practice for racist
purposes. That is not the situation here. Whatever the
origins of Florida’s law may be —and Florida argues
persuasively that its six-man jury law was untainted
by racism, Resp.Br.49-51—there is no argument that
other states that relied on Williams, like Arizona,
Connecticut, Indiana, Massachusetts, and Utah ,
adopted smaller juries for reasons related to race.
Florida notes the many salutary effects smaller juries
may have, Resp.Br.41-44, and one Justice has already
recognized that “some States have adopted smaller
criminal juries” for non-racist reasons, including costsavings, Khorrami, 143 S.Ct. at 27 (Gorsuch, J.,
dissenting from denial of certiorari).

30
D. The rule of Williams is workable.
Williams and its progeny —most significantly,
Ballew v. Georgia, 435 U.S. 223 (1978) , and Burch v.
Louisiana, 441 U.S. 130 (1979) —epitomize a
straightforward, bright-line rule: A state may convict
a defendant of a nonpetty offense with nothing less
than the unanimous verdict of  six jurors. This rule
“can be understood and applied in a consistent and
predictable manner.” Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 281. Nothing
about Williams’s rule is “unwieldy and inappropriate.”
Id. at 286.
E. Williams is consistent with the Court’s
other cases and has not had a negative
effect on other areas of the law.
Unlike precedents the Court has seen fit to
overrule, Williams is not “far out of step” with the
Court’s cases or been “all but limited to its facts .” Cf.
Slaughter, 146 S.Ct. at 2302. Nor has it “foster[ed] …
instability in the law.” Cf. Loper Bright Enter s. v.
Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 411 (2024). To the contrary,
this Court has repeatedly reaffirmed Williams’s
holding—and even extended it. Supra, at 26. And
despite Petitioner’s attempts to identify friction
between Williams and Ramos, Pet.Br.24-27, Williams
has been compatible with Ramos since at least 1979,
when the Court held that “conviction by a
nonunanimous six -member jury in a state criminal
trial for a nonpetty offense deprives an accused of his
constitutional right to trial by jury.” Burch, 441 U.S.
at 134.

31
Nor has Williams created difficulties elsewhere.
To the extent Williams can be blamed for Apodaca,
Ramos corrected that error  six years ago.  Williams
has not “led to the distortion of many important but
unrelated legal doctrines,” nor required “engineer[ed]
exceptions to longstanding background rules.” Dobbs,
597 U.S. at 286-87.
But reversing Williams would have negative
effects on other areas of the law. See Resp.Br.37-38,
44-49. Petitioner attempts to minimize the likely
aftershocks of overruling Williams. See Pet.Br.28. But
if Ramos should be read as having overruled Williams
sub silentio , id. at 24 -27, and reliance interests  are
insufficient to save Williams, id. at 37 -38, a formal
overruling of Williams will almost certainly  require
the overruling of additional precedents like Colgrove.
F. Williams has generated immense
reliance interests.
Most significantly, o verruling Williams would
“upend substantial reliance interests.” Dobbs, 597
U.S. at 287.  For over half a century, many States—
including seven today with respect to felonies —have
relied on this Court’s reasoned decision that six -
member juries satisfy the Constitution. Over 5 7
million people, or nearly 17% of the  U.S. population,
live in those States. And those States have built their
entire felony criminal justice system s on Williams.
The reliance interests here are precisely the
“prospective economic, regulatory, [and] social
disruption” costs that “litigants seeking to preserve
precedent usually invoke.” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 107.

32
Utah’s justice system is already under stress .
Supra, at 2. Overruling Williams portends potentially
devastating consequences for Utah:
1.  Lost convictions  and public safety .
Overruling Williams implicates hundreds of serious
felony convictions reaching back several decades. See
supra at 2-5.
2.  Infrastructure costs. Overruling Williams
will also force the State to spend millions of dollars to
build and modify  courtrooms, jury boxes, and
deliberation rooms . See Mow, supra, at 15  (even an
existing “shell courtroom space” cannot be finished
without $1,350,000).  Already, physical space is
severely limited. See id. (explaining one judge must
use a juvenile courtroom without a jury box and a
second must use virtual hearings or a juvenile
courtroom); id. (explaining court s may need to “set
more virtual hearings and virtual bench trials to free
up courtroom space”). Just two of the twenty -three
courtrooms at the Third District Courthouse in Salt
Lake City are equipped to seat 12 jurors, along with
just one of the eleven courtrooms in Utah County, the
State’s second most-populous.
The paucity of Petitioner’s historical record
provides no justification for unleashing such chaos or
imposing such costs.
Utah’s reliance interests are  even weightier
because this is not a situation where “Members of this
Court have long questioned [Williams’s] premises.” Cf.
Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 407.  Ramos could not have
put the States on notice because the Court said not a

33
word about Williams. And history supports the
rational concl usion that the  Sixth Amendment
requires unanimity but not a specific number of
jurors. See, e.g., Resp.Br.5, 8-10.
The Court has repeatedly declined to hear
challenges to Williams, and  the first call from the
Court to “reconsider” Williams came from a single
Justice in 2022. Khorrami, 143 S.Ct. at 23
(Gorsuch, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari).
Since that time, no other Justice has voiced concern
with Williams. So the States have not “been on notice
for years regarding this Court’s misgivings about”
Williams. Janus v. AFSCME , 585 U.S. 878, 927
(2018). Add the lack of any “badly fractured set of
opinions,” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 93 —and the Court’s
repeated reaffirmances and even extension of
Williams—and no State has had reason to believe its
practices “stood on shaky ground,” id. at 95 (plurality
op.). The states’ reliance on Williams is thus not only
“massive,” but also “entirely reasonable.” Id. at 1 64
(Alito, J., dissenting).
CONCLUSION
The judgment below should be affirmed.
